Behind the ride: How ROUVY brings real roads indoors

Every cyclist knows the feeling: the steady thrum of tyres on real tarmac, the new vistas and horizons that open up with each hill crested, the sense of exploring new frontiers… It’s why we love cycling – and why we don’t want it to stop when the weather turns.

Yet what if you could experience those same roads without leaving home? That’s the idea behind ROUVY, the real-world cycling app that brings actual roads and landscapes to your indoor trainer. Unlike platforms built around computer-generated worlds, ROUVY uses footage filmed on location, combined with augmented reality riders and accurate gradient data, to recreate the experience of riding the real thing.

And there’s a fascinating story behind every route. From scouting spectacular locations and filming in challenging conditions to transforming hours of footage into a rideable experience, bringing the world’s roads indoors takes a lot more than simply pointing a camera down the road.

Mission statement

Started in the small Czech town of Vimperk by brothers Petr and Jiří Samek in 2017, ROUVY’s mission was simple yet ambitious: to combine sport and technology to create the most realistic cycling experience possible. 

‘When we started ROUVY, our vision was to bring real-world cycling indoors. Today, that vision is still the same, but the technology has come a long way,’ says Vojtěch Hudeček, ROUVY’s routes project manager.

Fast forward to 2026 and it’s safe to say ROUVY’s vision has been realised. The company employs more than 100 people and has built a collection of thousands of routes in 130 countries covering nearly 400,000km. It partners with leading sporting events such as the Giro d’Italia and IRONMAN, works with elite athletes and teams, including WorldTour teams Lidl-Trek and Visma-Lease a Bike, and its routes are trusted for their authenticity and real-world accuracy.

For everyday riders, there’s a different appeal: the chance to explore the world and indulge your wanderlust through an ever-expanding library of riding locations. You can ride Grand Tour stages, ride iconic Alpine climbs or test yourself on gruelling Classics courses. Or you can venture further afield: rides in Morocco and India have recently been introduced, with Patagonia soon to follow. Near or far – with ROUVY, it’s up to you.

Wherever your virtual riding adventure takes you, each route is created with the same commitment to making it as close to actual riding as it gets. But how does ROUVY go about transforming a real-world road or iconic pass into an immersive, augmented reality route you can ride from home? Let’s take a look at how it all comes together.

How routes are built

ROUVY’s array of riding options covers every terrain and environment you can imagine, but it all starts with scouting.

‘Before we plan any filming trip, we always do extensive research to consider all pros and cons, evaluating the benefits of filming the planned routes,’ Hudeček says.

‘We look for routes that combine stunning scenery, iconic climbs and a great cycling experience. We focus on famous cycling destinations and major races, but we also love discovering hidden gems and exploring places that people normally don’t visit.’  

Once a target route is identified and fully researched, it’s time to capture the real-world footage that every ROUVY route is built on. Routes are filmed from start to finish using twin GoPros, high-quality video and imagery painstakingly captured through a custom mount attached to the front of a car. 

While the beauty of riding virtual routes from home is that you don’t have to worry about traffic, adverse weather or unforeseen obstacles, the same isn’t always the case when capturing those routes in the real world.

‘You never quite know what to expect when filming in places like India, Morocco or Patagonia,’ Hudeček says. ‘It could be unpredictable weather, heavy traffic, equipment problems, no GPS signal and other factors. That is part of the job – we need to react very quickly, but this all makes the adventure behind every route in those locations unforgettable and usually all those uneasy moments become the best stories from the trip.’

Once the raw footage has been captured, it’s then edited and produced back at the company’s headquarters in Prague by the ROUVY team. GPS data is converted into precise gradient and resistance profiles, then the final layer of virtual immersion is woven in: augmented reality (AR) through the addition of 3D riders, event banners and spatial realism elements. This is another key area that sets ROUVY apart from other platforms, and one that continues to develop as technology improves.

‘Our AR experience is more realistic, and creating routes is faster and more efficient,’ Hudeček says. ‘What hasn’t changed is our passion for bringing the world’s most beautiful roads to cyclists everywhere around the globe.’

Create your own Classic

A step-by-step guide to creating your own routes in ROUVY

From exotic travel destinations to world-famous climbs, ROUVY’s extensive global network of routes really does offer something for everyone. But what about your local training loop?  

‘With ROUVY Route Creator, anyone can now bring their favourite real-world roads to ROUVY and share them with cyclists from anywhere,’ ROUVY routes project manager Vojtěch Hudeček says.

That’s right – using the same tools ROUVY itself uses to create its routes, you too can film and upload routes and make them available to others within the platform. Here’s a quick run-through of how it works:

Step 1: Record your ride using a GoPro mounted on a car, bike or e-bike – ideally around 140-160cm off the ground and facing forward. Early or mid-morning is best from a lighting and traffic point of view, and if possible, footage should be 4K quality. Cloudy or overcast weather is fine, but avoid recording rides in wet conditions.

Step 2: Make sure your GoPro has GPS enabled, as this is essential for accurate gradient mapping. Keep the horizon level and centred, with a 50:50 split between sky and road. and record the entire ride in one continuous shot without pausing. Don’t drive close behind other vehicles, and maintain a steady road position and speed while filming.

Step 3: Import your MP4 video files into the ROUVY Route Creator software and shape your route into its final form using the editing tools. Define the start and finish points, remove unwanted sections and make sure the ride flows smoothly from beginning to end. Make sure the GPS data is correctly synced with your edited footage.

Step 4: Submit your route to be published to the global ROUVY community or keep it private should you wish to use it for personal training purposes only.

For more detailed information and tutorials on the ROUVY Route Creator, go to rouvy.com/route-creator
